triage.reason: Acute unilateral facial paralysis with a clear presentation; key teaching is distinguishing it from stroke and other causes of facial weakness by exam.

demographics: Slightly more common in females in some series
Incidence is similar across racial and ethnic groups
Most common cause of acute unilateral facial paralysis at any age

risk_factors.text: Pregnancy, especially the third trimester and early postpartum period
Recent upper respiratory infection or flu-like illness

family_history: Bell's palsy in a first-degree relative

chief_complaints.text: My face is drooping on one side
I can't close my eye on that side
Food and drink dribble out of the corner of my mouth

hpi.onset: Sudden, often noticed on waking or when smiling; reaches worst within 48–72 hours
hpi.duration: Symptoms at presentation are usually less than 3 days old
hpi.progression: Weakness progresses over 1–3 days, then plateaus; improvement typically begins within 2–3 weeks and complete recovery often occurs within 3–6 months
hpi.location: One side of the face, involving the forehead, eye and mouth
hpi.quality: Drooping and weakness of the whole half of the face, with inability to raise the eyebrow, close the eye tightly, or smile symmetrically
hpi.severity: Mild to severe; often described as complete inability to move that side of the face
aggravating: Attempting to smile or close the eye

associated_symptoms.text: Pain behind the ear on the affected side, often before the weakness
Impaired taste on the front of the tongue on the affected side
Increased sensitivity to sound on the affected side
Numbness or heaviness of the face, without true sensory loss

pertinent_negatives: Weakness or numbness of the arm or leg
Trouble walking or loss of balance
Rash or vesicles in or around the ear
Facial weakness that came on gradually over weeks
Weakness that comes and goes or is worse after activity

positives.text: Unilateral facial droop involving the forehead and lower face
Inability to close the eye on the affected side
Altered taste on the affected side of the tongue
Increased sensitivity to sound on the affected side

negatives: Numbness or sensory loss in the limbs
Loss of balance or trouble walking
argues_against: Weakness limited to the lower face with a spared forehead (suggests stroke)
Weakness of the limbs or speech disturbance (suggests stroke)

positives.text: Dryness or excessive tearing in the affected eye
Sensation of something in the eye

argues_against: Painful red eye with vision change (suggests other cause)

positives.text: Pain behind the ear on the affected side

negatives: Rash or vesicles in the ear canal or mouth
argues_against: Vesicles in the ear canal or mouth (suggests Ramsay Hunt syndrome)
High fever with rash (suggests infection or systemic illness)
Generalized weakness or fatigue (suggests neuromuscular disease)
Erythema migrans or vesicular rash (suggests Lyme disease or herpes zoster)

atypical.how_it_differs: Bell's palsy is less common in children; when it occurs, it may follow an ear infection or viral illness and recovery is usually good. Other causes such as Lyme disease should be considered in endemic areas.
Stroke becomes a much more likely cause of acute facial weakness, so the distinction between forehead-sparing weakness (stroke) and forehead-involving weakness (Bell's palsy) is critical.
Bell's palsy is more common in pregnancy, especially in the third trimester and early postpartum period. Presentation is otherwise similar, but treatment decisions must account for pregnancy.
Facial weakness may be due to opportunistic infection or malignancy rather than Bell's palsy; onset may be more gradual and other cranial nerves may be involved.
Diabetes is a risk factor for Bell's palsy, and diabetic patients may have a higher risk of incomplete recovery.

general.mild: Alert, well-appearing, in no distress; asymmetric smile but otherwise comfortable
general.moderate: Alert, mildly uncomfortable; eye on the affected side waters or feels dry, drools slightly with drinking
general.severe: Ill-at-ease, unable to close the affected eye, obvious facial asymmetry at rest, may hold a tissue to the mouth
general.critical: Not typical for Bell's palsy; if the patient is toxic-appearing, febrile, or has altered mental status, consider another diagnosis

findings.maneuver: Ask the patient to smile, show teeth, puff out the cheeks, and wrinkle the forehead
findings.finding: Unilateral weakness of the entire half of the face, involving both the upper face (forehead, eyebrow) and lower face (mouth, cheek)

findings.maneuver: Ask the patient to raise the eyebrows and wrinkle the forehead
findings.finding: Inability to raise the eyebrow or wrinkle the forehead on the affected side (upper facial weakness)

findings.maneuver: Ask the patient to close both eyes tightly while you try to open them
findings.finding: Inability to fully close the eye on the affected side; the eye rolls up (Bell's phenomenon) when closure is attempted

findings.maneuver: Inspect the face at rest and ask the patient to smile
findings.finding: Drooping of the corner of the mouth on the affected side; the nasolabial fold is flattened

findings.maneuver: Test strength in all four limbs and check gait
findings.finding: Normal strength and gait; no arm or leg weakness

findings.maneuver: Listen to the patient's spontaneous speech and ask them to repeat a sentence
findings.finding: Speech is clear and fluent; no dysarthria or aphasia

findings.maneuver: Test extraocular movements, visual fields, pupils, and hearing
findings.finding: Cranial nerves other than the facial nerve are intact; no diplopia, visual field cut, or hearing loss

findings.maneuver: Test taste on the anterior two-thirds of the tongue on both sides (e.g., with sugar or salt)
findings.finding: Decreased taste on the affected side of the tongue

findings.maneuver: Ask about sensitivity to sound or test with a tuning fork near the ear
findings.finding: Increased sensitivity to sound on the affected side

findings.maneuver: Palpate behind the ear on the affected side
findings.finding: Tenderness or pain behind the ear

findings.maneuver: Inspect the external ear canal, tympanic membrane, and oral mucosa
findings.finding: No vesicles or rash in the ear canal or mouth

findings.maneuver: Assess neck flexibility and perform Brudzinski and Kernig maneuvers if meningitis is a concern
findings.finding: No neck stiffness or meningeal signs

findings.maneuver: Inspect the skin, especially for a targetoid rash or vesicles
findings.finding: No rash, no erythema migrans, no vesicular lesions

findings.maneuver: Test facial sensation to light touch and pinprick on both sides
findings.finding: Sensation is intact; if the patient reports numbness, it does not follow a dermatomal or nerve distribution

findings.maneuver: Test deep tendon reflexes in the arms and legs

labs.caveat: Diabetes is a risk factor and may be newly found; hyperglycemia also worsens recovery. A normal glucose does not exclude the diagnosis.
Screens for undiagnosed diabetes, which is associated with Bell's palsy and poorer recovery.
Negative. Ordered in anyone who could be pregnant before starting corticosteroids or antivirals.

criteria.name: Clinical diagnosis of Bell's palsy
criteria.summary: Acute unilateral facial paralysis of unknown cause that involves the upper and lower face, develops over 1–3 days, and is not explained by another condition.
items: Sudden onset of unilateral facial weakness
Involvement of the forehead and lower face
No limb weakness, speech disturbance, or other neurologic signs

differential.name: Acute ischemic stroke
differential.why_considered: Acute facial weakness is a common stroke presentation and the most important alternative to exclude.
differential.trigger: Facial weakness that spares the forehead, or any limb weakness, speech disturbance, or other focal neurologic deficit.

history: Sudden onset, often maximal at once rather than progressing over 1–3 days
Weakness may involve the arm or leg
Vascular risk factors such as hypertension, diabetes, smoking, atrial fibrillation
exam: Forehead sparing: the patient can still wrinkle the forehead on the affected side
Weakness limited to the lower face
Arm or leg weakness, drift, or sensory loss
Gaze deviation or visual field cut
labs: Glucose and coagulation studies as part of stroke workup
imaging: Acute infarct on CT or MRI
Large vessel occlusion or restricted diffusion on MRI

differential.name: Ramsay Hunt syndrome
differential.why_considered: Herpes zoster of the geniculate ganglion causes acute unilateral facial paralysis that closely mimics Bell's palsy.
differential.trigger: Vesicles in the ear canal, on the pinna, or in the mouth, or severe ear pain with hearing loss.

history: Severe ear pain out of proportion to findings
Vesicular rash in or around the ear or mouth
exam: Vesicles in the external auditory canal, on the pinna, or on the oral mucosa
Sensorineural hearing loss on tuning fork testing
labs: Varicella-zoster virus PCR from vesicle fluid if diagnosis is uncertain
imaging: MRI may show facial and vestibulocochlear nerve enhancement

differential.name: Lyme disease
differential.why_considered: Lyme neuroborreliosis can cause unilateral or bilateral facial nerve palsy, especially in endemic areas.
differential.trigger: Tick exposure, erythema migrans rash, bilateral facial weakness, or residence in an endemic area.

history: Tick bite or exposure in an endemic area
Bilateral facial weakness is more common than in Bell's palsy
labs: Positive Lyme serology (ELISA with Western blot confirmation)
CSF lymphocytic pleocytosis if CNS involvement suspected
imaging: MRI may show meningeal or cranial nerve enhancement

differential.name: Otitis media with facial nerve involvement
differential.why_considered: Middle ear infection can inflame the facial nerve as it passes through the temporal bone.

history: Ear pain, fever, and recent upper respiratory infection
imaging: CT temporal bone if complications such as mastoiditis are suspected

differential.name: Temporal bone fracture
differential.why_considered: Trauma through the temporal bone can injure the facial nerve and cause acute facial paralysis.

history: Loss of consciousness or ear bleeding
exam: Hemotympanum, Battle sign, or raccoon eyes
Facial paralysis may be immediate or delayed

differential.name: Guillain-Barré syndrome
differential.why_considered: Can present with facial weakness, often bilateral, and ascending limb weakness.

history: Ascending weakness starting in the legs
exam: Reduced or absent deep tendon reflexes
labs: CSF albuminocytologic dissociation (elevated protein with normal cell count)
imaging: MRI spine may show nerve root enhancement

differential.name: Sarcoidosis
differential.why_considered: Neurosarcoidosis can cause facial nerve palsy, sometimes bilateral or recurrent.

history: Constitutional symptoms such as fever, weight loss, night sweats
imaging: Hilar lymphadenopathy on chest x-ray or CT

differential.name: Parotid gland tumor
differential.why_considered: A mass in the parotid gland can compress the facial nerve and cause gradual facial weakness.

history: Gradual onset over weeks to months
exam: Weakness may be progressive and involve only some branches of the facial nerve
imaging: Parotid mass on ultrasound, CT, or MRI

severity.mild: Incomplete weakness of the face; able to close the eye and smile with effort; no functional impairment.
severity.moderate: Complete or near-complete weakness of one side of the face; unable to close the eye tightly; drooling and difficulty with eating or drinking.
severity.severe: Complete paralysis with inability to close the eye, significant oral incompetence, and pain; risk of corneal injury.
severity.critical: Not typical for Bell's palsy; if the patient is toxic-appearing, febrile, or has altered mental status, consider another diagnosis.

red_flags.meaning: Suggests a central cause such as stroke rather than Bell's palsy.

red_flags.finding: Weakness of the arm or leg, or difficulty speaking
red_flags.meaning: Suggests stroke or another central nervous system lesion.

red_flags.finding: Fever, neck stiffness, or altered mental status
Vesicles in the ear canal or mouth
red_flags.meaning: Suggests Ramsay Hunt syndrome (herpes zoster oticus).
Suggests Lyme disease, Guillain-Barré syndrome, sarcoidosis, or another systemic cause.

red_flags.finding: Gradual onset over weeks or progressive weakness
red_flags.meaning: Suggests a tumor or another structural cause.

complications.name: Corneal injury (exposure keratitis, ulceration)
clues: Eye redness, pain, or foreign body sensation

complications.name: Incomplete recovery with residual facial weakness or synkinesis
clues: Involuntary facial movements with voluntary ones

special_populations.differences: Bell's palsy is less common in children; when it occurs, it may follow an ear infection or viral illness and recovery is usually good. Other causes such as Lyme disease should be considered in endemic areas.
Stroke becomes a much more likely cause of acute facial weakness, so the distinction between forehead-sparing weakness (stroke) and forehead-involving weakness (Bell's palsy) is critical.
Bell's palsy is more common in pregnancy, especially in the third trimester and early postpartum period. Presentation is otherwise similar, but treatment decisions must account for pregnancy.
Facial weakness may be due to opportunistic infection or malignancy rather than Bell's palsy; onset may be more gradual and other cranial nerves may be involved.

key_questions.question: When did the weakness start, and how fast did it get to its worst?
key_questions.looking_for: Sudden onset reaching worst within 48–72 hours; gradual progression over weeks suggests a tumor or another structural cause

key_questions.question: Is the weakness on one side or both sides?
key_questions.looking_for: One side; bilateral weakness suggests Lyme disease, Guillain-Barré syndrome, or sarcoidosis

key_questions.question: Can you raise your eyebrow and wrinkle your forehead on that side?
key_questions.looking_for: Inability to wrinkle the forehead (upper face involved); a spared forehead points to stroke

key_questions.question: Can you close that eye completely?
key_questions.looking_for: Incomplete eye closure, which risks corneal injury and drives eye care

key_questions.question: Do you have any weakness, numbness, or clumsiness in your arm or leg?
key_questions.looking_for: Absent; limb weakness suggests stroke or another central lesion

key_questions.question: Any trouble speaking, understanding speech, or swallowing?
key_questions.looking_for: Absent; present suggests stroke or brainstem involvement

key_questions.question: Did you have pain behind your ear before the weakness started?
key_questions.looking_for: Postauricular pain, which commonly precedes Bell's palsy

key_questions.question: Has your sense of taste changed, or does sound seem unusually loud on that side?
key_questions.looking_for: Altered taste on the front of the tongue or hyperacusis, supporting facial nerve involvement

key_questions.question: Any rash, blisters, or sores in or around your ear or mouth?
key_questions.looking_for: Vesicles suggest Ramsay Hunt syndrome (herpes zoster oticus)

key_questions.question: Any hearing loss, ringing in the ear, or spinning sensation?
key_questions.looking_for: Absent; hearing loss or vertigo suggests Ramsay Hunt syndrome or another cause

key_questions.question: Have you had a recent cold, flu, or other viral illness?
key_questions.looking_for: Recent upper respiratory infection, a common trigger

key_questions.question: Have you had a tick bite, a rash, or been in an area where Lyme disease is common?
key_questions.looking_for: Tick exposure or erythema migrans, which points to Lyme disease

key_questions.question: Do you have diabetes, or are you pregnant or recently postpartum?
key_questions.looking_for: Diabetes or pregnancy, both risk factors for Bell's palsy and relevant to treatment

key_questions.question: Have you ever had facial weakness like this before?
key_questions.looking_for: Recurrent episodes suggest an alternative diagnosis such as sarcoidosis or a structural lesion

key_questions.question: Any fever, neck stiffness, or severe headache?
key_questions.looking_for: Absent; present suggests meningitis or encephalitis

key_questions.question: Any recent head injury or trauma to the ear?
key_questions.looking_for: Absent; trauma suggests temporal bone fracture

key_questions.question: Does anyone in your family have Bell's palsy?
key_questions.looking_for: Family history, a weak risk factor

reasoning_points: Acute unilateral facial weakness that involves both the upper face (forehead, eyebrow) and lower face
Onset is sudden and progresses over 1–3 days, then plateaus
No limb weakness, no speech disturbance, and no other cranial nerve deficits
Postauricular pain, altered taste on the anterior tongue, or hyperacusis may accompany the weakness
No vesicles in the ear or mouth, ruling out Ramsay Hunt syndrome
No tick exposure or rash, and no bilateral weakness, making Lyme disease less likely
No fever, neck stiffness, or altered mental status, arguing against meningitis or encephalitis
The presentation is not explained by stroke, tumor, trauma, or another structural cause

easy: Young adult with sudden one-sided facial droop noticed on waking
Forehead and lower face both involved, with inability to close the eye
Postauricular pain and altered taste on the affected side
No limb weakness, speech difficulty, or other cranial nerve findings
medium: Older adult with vascular risk factors, requiring careful distinction from stroke
Patient with diabetes or pregnancy, where risk is higher and treatment must be adjusted
Mild weakness that is easy to overlook without testing forehead wrinkling and eye closure
Recent viral illness with subtle associated symptoms such as hyperacusis
hard: Bilateral facial weakness suggesting Lyme disease, Guillain-Barré syndrome, or sarcoidosis
Gradual or progressive weakness over weeks suggesting a parotid tumor or other structural cause
Vesicles in the ear canal or mouth indicating Ramsay Hunt syndrome
Recurrent episodes or additional cranial nerve deficits suggesting an alternative diagnosis
Facial weakness after head trauma suggesting temporal bone fracture
